updates.body:
On November 9, 2026, from 09:23 to 11:40 UTC, one of our job queue clusters was degraded, delaying webhook deliveries, Actions workflow runs, and Dependabot and dependency graph updates. Until mitigation at 10:37 UTC, an average of 26% of webhook deliveries were delayed, peaking at 30%, and the backlog cleared by 11:40 UTC. Some deliveries were delayed by up to 3.5 hours, and delays for a small share began as early as 01:00 UTC. Actions skips events older than 30 minutes, so some workflow runs did not start.

The incident was caused by a degraded host that had slowed one of the cluster's Kafka brokers since November 7. The broker stopped reporting the metrics our alerts rely on, so we did not identify it until it stalled the cluster on November 9.

We mitigated the incident by removing the broker from service. We have since added an alert that pages us within 30 minutes when a host slows a broker this way, so we can remove the broker before it affects customers.

updates.body:
On November 9, 2026, between 18:07 and 18:59 UTC, GitHub Actions experienced degraded performance. During this time, some customers saw workflow runs fail to start, update or report status correctly. An average of 28% of workflow runs were affected, peaking at 65% during the worst period of the incident. Once Actions services recovered, some jobs were left in a state that limited available concurrency until the runs were released.

The incident occurred during a planned migration of a core Actions database from GitHub’s datacenter to a new cloud region. After the migration completed, we shifted Actions service traffic to the new region. The volume of requests exceeded the capacity and rate limits configured there, so a portion of requests were rejected and workflow updates failed. Dependent services, including Webhooks, Pages and Copilot code review, saw secondary impact.

We mitigated impact by shifting some of the traffic back to the original region, allowing service traffic to remain within the configured limits. We then increased capacity and rate limits in the new region before gradually shifting traffic back. While this was a one-time migration event for this cluster that is now complete, we are improving how we validate capacity and limits before shifting traffic during remaining migrations, including shifting traffic in smaller steps. To address the stuck runs left after the incident, we are improving our ability to detect and mitigate these runs for future cases as well as readying an API to enable customers to address this themselves.

updates.body:
On November 10, 2026, from approximately 15:00 UTC to 17:55 UTC, GitHub experienced degraded performance affecting repository pages, pull requests, and GitHub Actions. Customers may have seen slow or failed page loads and delays processing pull request updates and merges. Some pull requests continued to display an earlier source-branch commit after the broader service degradation ended. GitHub Actions workflows were delayed for approximately 1.8% of events, peaking at about 7% between 16:30 and 16:50 UTC. Delays were typically 1.5 to 3.5 minutes, up to 10 minutes. Approximately 0.09% of pull request events did not start their workflows and needed to be re-triggered.

The degradation resulted from overload in the shared infrastructure that supports Git operations. Recent changes increased background processing and the work required to compute pull request merges, adding pressure to the same systems used by customer-facing requests. We mitigated the incident by disabling a recent merge-processing optimization, pausing background analysis, and temporarily limiting lower-priority traffic. The temporary limits also restricted access to commit pages for users who were not signed in. Background processing continued to catch up after service health recovered.

We have reduced repeated repository-analysis work and are adding workload-level concurrency controls to better protect customer-facing requests. We are also improving our procedures for safely reducing background load and making pull request synchronization more resilient to temporary failures.

updates.body:
On November 11, 2026, from 20:05 to 21:02 UTC, customers experienced delayed or failed Actions workflow starts, webhook errors and delivery delays, slower GitHub Apps API requests, and reduced availability of Copilot features, including Code Review. GitHub Pages builds were also delayed.

Nearly all GitHub Actions runs triggered between 20:18 and 20:55 UTC were delayed or failed, leaving approximately 3.4 million partially created runs that are being canceled. No GitHub Pages deployments completed during the incident. In the Central US data residency stamp, between 20:06 and 20:50 UTC, about 63% of webhook API requests failed and 27% of deliveries were not recorded; those deliveries reached their destinations but remain unavailable to view or redeliver. Between approximately 20:20 and 21:00 UTC, Copilot code review on github.com completed 87% fewer reviews than normal and some other Copilot features were also unavailable.

The disruption was caused by an Azure Cosmos DB regional outage affecting database accounts used by these services. Per Cosmos’s RCA, a configuration change to the Central US gateways exposed a latent race condition under a specific high-load traffic pattern, causing gateway crashes and health-probe failures. Cosmos mitigated by rolling back the change. Service health recovered around 21:02 UTC, and the queued Actions backlog finished processing by 21:21 UTC.

Our follow-up work focuses on validating regional database failover across affected services and developing tested recovery procedures. We are also improving recovery tools to quickly clear stuck Actions checks and runs after incidents so they do not remain uncancelable or block pull request merges.

We are working with our database provider to understand the cause and are improving our playbooks to detect degradations more quickly.

updates.body:
On November 16, 2026, between 09:30 and 15:55 UTC, some pull request merges on GitHub timed out. On average, 2.9% of merge attempts timed out, with a peak of 7.1% at 15:17 UTC. Some GitHub Actions workflow runs triggered by pull requests were also delayed. Git operations such as push and fetch stayed available, with higher latency. This was a repeat of a shorter event on November 13, between 13:15 and 17:50 UTC, when 1.7% of merges timed out.

Both events had the same cause: some of the storage servers that hold Git repository data reached their disk read bandwidth limits. A merge must be written to every copy of a repository, so one overloaded server slowed merges for every repository it hosts. Read load on these servers had been growing as part of a planned move of repositories to new infrastructure. A disk configuration setting on those servers also made them read far more data than necessary, which cut their usable bandwidth roughly in half. We mitigated the incident by correcting that setting and moving some load away from the busiest servers.

The corrected setting is now applied permanently across our storage fleet. We are adding storage capacity in the affected region and alerting on per-server disk bandwidth so we catch saturation before it affects customers. Sustained merge timeouts will now page our on-call engineers directly. We are also adding capacity checks before moving repositories or traffic onto new infrastructure.

This was a repeat of a shorter event on November 13, between 13:15 and 17:50 UTC, when 1.7% of merges timed out.

Both events had the same cause: some of the storage servers that hold Git repository data reached their disk read bandwidth limits. A merge must be written to every copy of a repository, so one overloaded server slowed merges for every repository it hosts. Read load on these servers had been growing as part of a planned move of repositories to new infrastructure. A disk configuration setting on those servers also made them read far more data than necessary, which cut their usable bandwidth roughly in half. We mitigated the incident by correcting that setting and moving some load away from the busiest servers.

The corrected setting is now applied permanently across our storage fleet. We are adding storage capacity in the affected region and alerting on per-server disk bandwidth so we catch saturation before it affects customers. Sustained merge timeouts will now page our on-call engineers directly. We are also adding capacity checks before moving repositories or traffic onto new infrastructure.

Between November 5, 2026, at 18:02 UTC and November 19, 2026, at 18:05 UTC, GitHub users experienced unexpected expiration of their web browser sessions despite continued activity, requiring them to login. An authentication change introduced an issue that caused web requests to bypass the session activity updates and cookie renewal that normally extend session lifetime. Affected sessions consequently expired when they reached their initial expiration time.

We mitigated the incident by deploying a fix to ensure that continued web activity renews session expiration and browser cookies.

We are adding monitoring to detect unexpected drops in session renewal activity, helping us catch similar issues sooner and reduce their impact on users.

incidents.title: On-demand reports issues

updates.body:
Some agents may request on-demand Income Tax lodgment status and outstanding Activity Statement reports that subsequently are not returned. Tax agents using Practice Management Software can access the Income Tax report through their software along with a similar report for Activity Statements.

We are acutely aware that BAS and some Tax agents are especially impacted by the failure of Activity Statement reports in OSFA. Hence, we are working to resolve this issue as a priority.

Some agents may request on-demand Income Tax lodgment status and outstanding Activity Statement reports that subsequently are not returned. Tax agents using Practice Management Software can access the Income Tax report through their software along with a similar report for Activity Statements.

We are acutely aware that BAS and some Tax agents are especially impacted by the failure of Activity Statement reports in OSFA. Hence, we are working to resolve this issue as a priority.

updates.body:
### **SUMMARY**

We understand the importance of providing reliable and consistent service to our valued customers. On July 6, 2023, from 03:52 to 15:11 UTC, we experienced an issue with an upgraded version of a third-party tool that functions as our internal artifact management system. Despite our monitoring system identifying the incident within two minutes, this issue led to the degradation of the scaling capabilities of our internal hosting platform, resulting in service degradation or outages for customers of Atlassian cloud.

In response to this situation, we are taking immediate measures to enhance the stability of our system and prevent similar issues from re-occurring.

### **IMPACT**

This incident affected multiple regions and products due to the diminished scaling capabilities of our internal hosting platform. In most products and offerings, customers faced reduced functionality, slower response times, and limited access to specific features.

### **ROOT CAUSE**

The root cause of the incident was the introduction of new functionality in a third-party tool that functions as our internal artifact management system. It led to an unexpected increase in the load on the primary database of the artifact system.

Upon identifying and localizing the problem, we promptly adjusted the system configuration to regain stability.

### **REMEDIAL ACTIONS PLAN & NEXT STEPS**

Over the next months, we will enact a temporary freeze on non-critical upgrades of the artifact management system, and we will focus our efforts on three high-priority initiatives:

1. **Enhancing system scaling:** We prioritized work ensuring that downtime in a critical infrastructure component does not affect the scaling of other components. We expect to complete this initiative within the next two months.
2. **Reducing interdependencies:** We are working to mitigate the risk of potential cascading failures by ensuring that significant system components are able to operate independently in the case of issues. Initiatives 1 and 2 are already in progress but have been given priority to be completed as soon as possible.
3. **Strengthening testing procedures:** Alongside these initiatives, we are addressing the need for even more stringent testing procedures than we already have in place to prevent potential issues in future updates. We are committed to collaborating closely with our technology partners to ensure the most optimal experience for our customers.

We apologize for any inconvenience caused by this incident and appreciate your understanding. Our team is dedicated to continually improving our systems and processes to provide you with the exceptional service you deserve. Thank you for your continued support and trust in us.

Sincerely,

Atlassian Customer Support

On July 6, 2023, from 03:52 to 15:11 UTC, we experienced an issue with an upgraded version of a third-party tool that functions as our internal artifact management system. Despite our monitoring system identifying the incident within two minutes, this issue led to the degradation of the scaling capabilities of our internal hosting platform, resulting in service degradation or outages for customers of Atlassian cloud.

In response to this situation, we are taking immediate measures to enhance the stability of our system and prevent similar issues from re-occurring.

### **IMPACT**

This incident affected multiple regions and products due to the diminished scaling capabilities of our internal hosting platform. In most products and offerings, customers faced reduced functionality, slower response times, and limited access to specific features.

### **ROOT CAUSE**

The root cause of the incident was the introduction of new functionality in a third-party tool that functions as our internal artifact management system. It led to an unexpected increase in the load on the primary database of the artifact system.

Upon identifying and localizing the problem, we promptly adjusted the system configuration to regain stability.

### **REMEDIAL ACTIONS PLAN & NEXT STEPS**

Over the next months, we will enact a temporary freeze on non-critical upgrades of the artifact management system, and we will focus our efforts on three high-priority initiatives:

1. **Enhancing system scaling:** We prioritized work ensuring that downtime in a critical infrastructure component does not affect the scaling of other components. We expect to complete this initiative within the next two months.
2. **Reducing interdependencies:** We are working to mitigate the risk of potential cascading failures by ensuring that significant system components are able to operate independently in the case of issues. Initiatives 1 and 2 are already in progress but have been given priority to be completed as soon as possible.
3. **Strengthening testing procedures:** Alongside these initiatives, we are addressing the need for even more stringent testing procedures than we already have in place to prevent potential issues in future updates. We are committed to collaborating closely with our technology partners to ensure the most optimal experience for our customers.

We apologize for any inconvenience caused by this incident and appreciate your understanding. Our team is dedicated to continually improving our systems and processes to provide you with the exceptional service you deserve. Thank you for your continued support and trust in us.

Sincerely,

Atlassian Customer Support

updates.body:
### **SUMMARY**

On Dec 18, 2023, between 12:29 p.m. and 3:35 p.m. UTC, Dec 18, 2023, Atlassian's cloud customers using Atlas, Bitbucket Cloud, Compass, Confluence Cloud, Jira Service Management, Jira Software, Jira Work Management, Jira Product Discovery products were unable to search for users or use the "@mention" functionality. Customers' user search results failed or were delayed as Atlassian's service returning user search results was degraded in several regions.

The incident originated from a computationally intensive operation that was triggered multiple times in rapid succession, resulting in degraded performance of Atlassian's user search service across several regions. Notably, customers in the EU west region were most affected. The incident was detected within 2 minutes by automated monitoring, and our team promptly took action by recovering unhealthy systems and scaling up the service's infrastructure temporarily. The resolution process concluded in 3 hours and 06 minutes.

### **IMPACT**

The overall impact was between Dec 18, 2023, between 12:29 p.m. UTC and Dec 18, 2023, 3:35 p.m. UTC. The Incident caused service disruption to cloud customers worldwide. Customers experienced delayed or failed user searches when using the following Atlassian cloud products:

* Atlas
* Bitbucket Cloud
* Compass
* Confluence Cloud
* Jira Service Management
* Jira Software
* Jira Work Management
* Jira Product Discovery

### **ROOT CAUSE**

The incident stemmed from Atlassian's user search service receiving commands to process multiple computationally intensive operations in rapid succession. updates.body:
### **Summary**

On February 14, 2024, between 20:05 UTC and 23:03 UTC, Atlassian customers on the following cloud products encountered a service disruption: Access, Atlas, Atlassian Analytics, Bitbucket, Compass, Confluence, Ecosystem apps, Jira Service Management, Jira Software, Jira Work Management, Jira Product Discovery, Opsgenie, StatusPage, and Trello.

As part of a security and compliance uplift, we had scheduled the deletion of unused and legacy domain names used for internal service-to-service connections. Active domain names were incorrectly deleted during this event. This impacted all cloud customers across all regions. The issue was identified and resolved through the rollback of the faulty deployment to restore the domain names and Atlassian systems to a stable state. The time to resolution was two hours and 58 minutes.

### **IMPACT**

External customers started reporting issues with Atlassian cloud products at 20:52 UTC. The impact of the failed change led to performance degradation or in some cases, complete service disruption. Symptoms experienced by end-users were unsuccessful page loads and/or failed interactions with our cloud products.

### **ROOT CAUSE**

As part of a security and compliance uplift, we had scheduled the deletion of unused and legacy domain names that were being used for internal service-to-service connections. Active domain names were incorrectly deleted during this operation.

### **REMEDIAL ACTIONS PLAN & NEXT STEPS**

We know that outages impact your productivity. The detection was delayed because existing testing & monitoring focused on service health rather than the entire system’s availability.

To prevent a recurrence of this type of incident, we are implementing the following improvement measures:

* Canary checks to monitor the entire system availability.
* Faster rollback procedures for this type of service impact.
* Stricter change control procedures for infrastructure modifications.
* Migration of all DNS records to centralised management and stricter access controls on modification to DNS records.

We apologize to customers whose services were impacted during this incident; we are taking immediate steps to improve the platform’s performance and availability.

‌

Thanks,

Atlassian Customer Support
